title: Open Source Contribution Basics: Git, GitHub & Pull Requests
subtitle: Ship a real PR this month — not a lecture about one.
description: A 3-week studio: official GitHub how-tos, two hands-on labs (GitHub Skills + First Contributions), then a real issue you can actually open a pull request for. Quizzes check the commands; assignments check that you did the work.
outcomes: First PR shipped — a public pull request URL from this month

modules.title: Week 1: Do the GitHub flow yourself
modules.summary: Watch the 4-minute PR, then leave a public PR URL in the assignment.

lessons.title: What is GitHub? (official, 2 min)
lessons.description: GitHub’s own walkthrough of a repo: where the code lives, how a team shares it, and why the Pull requests tab exists.

lessons.title: Create a pull request in 4 minutes | GitHub for Beginners
lessons.description: Official screen-share: branch, commit, push, Compare & pull request, then write a title a reviewer can scan. Pause and do it on your account.

lessons.title: How to Find GitHub Repos to Contribute To
lessons.description: Use GitHub search, topics, and the good-first-issue label to find active projects instead of guessing.

lessons.title: How to Find Good First Issues in Open Source
lessons.description: Beginner-friendly labels, maintainer channels, and aggregators so you are not staring at a 1,700-issue backlog.

lessons.title: Git Cheat Sheet & PR Workflow Handbook
lessons.description: GitHub’s education cheat sheet: status, branch, commit, remotes, and the commands you will use on every PR. Keep it open during the lab.

lessons.title: Lab: Open your first pull request
lessons.description: Complete GitHub Skills, then land a practice PR on First Contributions. Paste the URLs — watching does not count.

assignment.brief: Do the work on GitHub, then write what you actually ran. Two labs: GitHub Skills ‘Introduction to GitHub’ (https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-github) and First Contributions (https://github.com/firstcontributions/first-contributions). Either merged or still open is fine.
assignment.deliverable: A public PR URL plus the commands you used.

fields.label: GitHub Skills repo or completion URL
fields.hint: Copy the exercise to your account, finish the four steps (branch, commit, PR, merge), then paste that repo URL.

fields.label: Your First Contributions (or Skills) pull request URL
fields.hint: Must be a pull request, not the repo homepage.

fields.label: What you changed, in one sentence
fields.placeholder: Added my name to Contributors.md on a branch called …
fields.hint: If you cannot name the file and the branch, you did not finish the lab.

fields.label: Commands you actually ran
fields.placeholder:
git clone …
git checkout -b …
git add …
git commit -m …
git push origin …
fields.hint: Paste the real sequence, including the one that failed and what you did next.

checklist: The PR URL opens in an incognito window.
You named a file and a branch, not ‘I followed the video’.
The command list includes clone or fork, a branch, commit, and push.

lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Git & Contribution Basics
lessons.description: Branching, issue linking, and how you actually find a first issue.

questions.prompt: Which command creates a new feature branch and switches to it in one step?

options.text: git branch fix/issue-10
git checkout -b fix/issue-10
git commit -m 'fix issue'
git push origin main

questions.explanation: `git checkout -b fix/issue-10` (or `git switch -c`) creates the branch and checks it out. `git branch` only creates it; you would still need to switch.

questions.prompt: In a pull request body, how do you link the work to GitHub issue 42 so the issue can close when the PR merges?

options.text: Write the issue number only: 42
Use a closing keyword: Fixes #42
Tag @github
Put the issue URL in a commit that never gets pushed

questions.explanation: `Fixes #42`, `Closes #42`, or `Resolves #42` links the PR to the issue and can auto-close it on merge.

questions.prompt: You want beginner issues in Python on GitHub. Which search is the most useful starting point?

options.text: stars:>100000 is:closed
language:python label:"good first issue" state:open
filename:password.txt
org:ghost

questions.explanation: Filter by language plus a newcomer label and open state. Huge starred + closed searches hide the work you can actually take.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that belongs in a first contribution.

options.text: Read README and CONTRIBUTING before writing code.
Work on a branch, not on upstream main.
Force-push to the project's main branch.
Comment on the issue before (or as) you start, if the project asks you to.

questions.explanation: Read the room, branch off main, talk to maintainers. Never force-push someone else's default branch.

modules.title: Week 2: Fix a conflict with your own hands
modules.summary: SSH, rebase vs merge, then the GitHub Skills conflict lab — not a 60-minute crash course.

lessons.title: GitHub for Beginners: SSH, PAT, conflicts, sync a fork
lessons.description: GitHub engineers screen-share the stuff that actually blocks first-timers: add an SSH key, mint a PAT, resolve a conflict in the PR UI, sync a fork, and review a diff.

lessons.title: Git Branches, Merge, and Rebase (do this in a throwaway repo)
lessons.description: Create two branches, collide on the same line, merge, then rebase your feature onto updated main. Pause and reproduce each command locally.

lessons.title: GitHub Git Cheat Sheet
lessons.description: Keep this open while you resolve conflicts: fetch, merge, rebase, stash, and log.

lessons.title: Lab: Resolve a merge conflict
lessons.description: Run GitHub Skills ‘Resolve merge conflicts’, then write what the markers meant and what you kept.

assignment.brief: Start the official lab: https://github.com/skills/resolve-merge-conflicts (about 30 minutes). You can also manufacture a conflict in a throwaway repo: two branches, same line, different words, then merge.
assignment.deliverable: Proof you resolved a conflict, plus the final file contents in your own words.

fields.label: Skills lab repo or the PR where you resolved the conflict
fields.hint: A repo or PR link a classmate could open.

fields.label: What you saw and what you kept
fields.placeholder: <<<<<<< HEAD had … / ======= / >>>>>>> feature had … I kept … because …
fields.hint: Quote the two sides. ‘I clicked resolve’ is not enough.

fields.label: On your next feature branch, rebase or merge — and why
fields.placeholder: I would rebase onto latest main before the PR because…
fields.hint: Rebase your unpushed solo branch. Do not rebase a shared main.

checklist: You linked a repo or PR, not a docs page.
You described both sides of the conflict, not only the winner.
You said when you would not rebase.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: Conflicts & History
lessons.description: Conflict markers, rebase vs merge, and what not to rewrite.

questions.prompt: You open a file after a failed merge and see <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. What should you do?

options.text: Commit immediately; Git already picked a winner.
Edit the file to the intended result, delete the markers, then add and commit.
Delete the repository and clone again.
Run git push --force on main.

questions.explanation: Conflict markers are a pause, not a result. You choose the code, remove the markers, then stage and commit the resolution.

questions.prompt: When is `git rebase` a reasonable tool on your own feature branch?

options.text: To replay your commits on top of latest main before you open a PR.
To rewrite commits already on the shared main branch.
To delete GitHub issues.
To skip code review.

questions.explanation: Rebase your unpushed (or solo) feature branch onto updated main. Do not rebase public history others already pulled.

options.text: git fetch updates your remote-tracking branches without merging.
A merge commit records that two histories were joined.
git push --force on origin/main is standard for first-time contributors.
Small, focused commits are easier to review than one giant dump.

questions.explanation: Fetch is safe. Merge commits are a record. Force-pushing main is how you become unwelcome. Small diffs review faster.

modules.title: Week 3: Open a PR a maintainer can review
modules.summary: Pick a live issue, write the PR body, and draft the comment you will post.

lessons.title: Step-by-step: contribute to open source
lessons.description: Fork, clone, branch, commit, push, and open the PR — the full loop with the habits maintainers expect. Follow along on a real repo, not a notepad.

lessons.title: Studio: Claim a real issue and draft the PR
lessons.description: Find an open good-first-issue, extract the project’s rules, and write the PR description you would submit.

assignment.brief: Search `label:"good first issue" state:open` in a language you know. Read README + CONTRIBUTING. You do not have to merge this week — you do have to pick a real issue and write the artifacts a maintainer would read.
assignment.deliverable: Issue URL, three project rules, a PR body, and the issue comment you will post.

fields.label: Issue URL and why this one is sized for you
fields.placeholder: https://github.com/org/repo/issues/123 — it asks for … and the file to touch is …
fields.hint: Name the file or area. ‘It said good first issue’ is not a reason.

fields.label: Three rules from README / CONTRIBUTING you will follow
fields.placeholder:
1. Branch naming…
2. How to claim an issue…
3. Tests / DCO / PR template…
fields.hint: Quote the project, not generic Git advice.

fields.label: Draft PR title + body
fields.placeholder:
Title: Fix typo in …

## What
## Why
## How I tested
Fixes #123
fields.hint: Include a closing keyword if the issue should close on merge.

fields.label: The issue comment you will post
fields.placeholder: Hi — I’d like to take this. I will … Is this still open?
fields.hint: Short, specific, and ask if it is free. No ‘please assign me this thank you’ spam.

checklist: The issue URL is open on GitHub today.
The three rules came from that repo’s docs.
The PR body says what, why, how you tested, and Fixes #n.
The comment is something you would actually post.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Pull Requests
lessons.description: What a reviewable PR looks like.

questions.prompt: A reviewable first PR usually is:

options.text: A rewrite of the entire codebase.
Small, tested, and described, with the related issue linked.
Pushed straight to upstream main.
Opened without a description so reviewers 'see the code'.

questions.explanation: Maintainers merge small, explained changes. Giant surprise rewrites stall.

questions.prompt: CI on your PR is red. Best next move?

options.text: Ask for merge anyway; CI is optional.
Read the failing job, fix it on your branch, and push a follow-up commit.
Close the repo.
Open five more PRs to distract from it.

questions.explanation: Green checks are part of the contribution. Fix the branch; don't argue with the required workflow.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about review.

options.text: Review comments are normal; reply and/or push fixes.
You should discuss scope on the issue if the fix grows.
Changing files the issue never mentioned, silently, is a gift.
A polite, specific PR description saves a round of questions.

questions.explanation: Review is collaboration. Stay on scope unless you agree otherwise. Write like a teammate.
